title: The Overlap Count
question: In a full day, how many times do the hour and minute hands of a working analog clock lie exactly on top of each other?
correctExplanation: Right. The hands align eleven times per twelve-hour sweep, and a full day runs two sweeps.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 22. Intuition says twenty-four, but each twelve-hour cycle fits only eleven alignments — the minute hand must catch up on a moving target, not a stationary one. Two cycles give twenty-two.
lessonContent:
Clock-hand puzzles are pursuit problems in disguise.
The minute hand chases a target moving at one twelfth its speed.
Count alignments per cycle, then multiply cycles.
Relative speed, not absolute speed, settles every catch-up question.

title: Fifteen Past
question: At exactly 3:15, what is the angle in degrees between the hour hand and the minute hand?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The minute hand sits at 90 degrees while the hour hand has crept a quarter of the way from three toward four: 97.5 minus 90.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7.5 degrees. The trap assumes the hour hand sits frozen on the three, but it moves half a degree every minute. At fifteen past it has advanced 7.5 degrees beyond the three.
lessonContent:
Both clock hands move; only their speeds differ.
The hour hand advances half a degree per minute.
Compute each hand's position separately before subtracting.
Frozen-hour-hand assumptions cause most wrong answers.

title: A Minute a Day
question: A clock loses exactly one minute every day. If set correctly now, after how many days will it next show the correct time again?
correctExplanation: Right. The display must be off by a full twelve hours — 720 minutes — before it coincides with reality again.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 720 days. A stopped or drifting clock shows the right time only when its error wraps around to a full twelve-hour offset. Losing one minute daily needs 720 days to accumulate that offset.
lessonContent:
Drifting clocks resync only at full twelve-hour error offsets.
Break the question into the error accumulated per day and the target offset.
Twelve hours equals 720 minutes — a useful conversion to memorize.
Drift problems are slow-motion modular arithmetic.

title: Twelve Strikes
question: A clock takes 6 seconds to strike six o'clock, striking at even intervals. How many seconds pass while it strikes twelve?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Six strikes contain five intervals of 1.2 seconds each; twelve strikes contain eleven intervals, and eleven times 1.2 gives 13.2.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 13.2 seconds. The trap doubles six to twelve seconds, but intervals live between strikes, not on them. Count the gaps — always one fewer than the strikes.
lessonContent:
Interval problems count gaps, not events.
N events carry N minus one intervals.
Fence-post counting errors plague clocks, posts, and floors alike.
State what an interval connects before computing speed.

title: Forty-Five Days
question: Today is Sunday. What day of the week will it be exactly 45 days from now?
correctExplanation: Right. Forty-five divided by seven leaves three, and three days after Sunday is Wednesday.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is Wednesday. Whole weeks vanish — only the remainder matters. Forty-five contains six weeks plus three days, so count forward just three days from Sunday.
lessonContent:
Weekday puzzles run on remainders modulo seven.
Whole weeks cancel themselves completely.
Reduce the count first, then count forward.
The remainder is the entire answer.

title: Month Math
question: Counting eight months forward from March, which month do you land in?
correctExplanation: Exactly. April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November — eight hops lands on the eleventh month.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is November. March plus eight months walks through the whole summer to November. Month arithmetic is hopping, not adding — count the landings, not the starting post.
lessonContent:
Month arithmetic counts hops, not fence posts.
Starting months are excluded from the count.
Writing the sequence out loud beats mental shortcuts.
Off-by-one errors dominate calendar puzzles.

title: Fridays Maximum
question: What is the greatest number of Fridays a single calendar month can contain?
correctExplanation: Right. A 31-day month spans five of some weekday whenever it starts on that weekday's eve — at most five of any day.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Thirty-one days equal four full weeks plus three days, so at most one weekday appears five times. Six would need more than thirty-five days.
lessonContent:
Month lengths are four weeks plus a remainder of two or three days.
Only the remainder days can appear a fifth time.
Maximum-count questions are division with leftovers.
Thirty-one days cap every weekday at five.

title: The Mirror Time
question: An analog clock read in a mirror appears to show 3:40. What time does the clock actually show?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Mirrored positions reflect across the twelve-six axis, and the true time plus the mirror time always sum to twelve hours minus the reading quirk — here 8:20 pairs with 3:40.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8:20. A mirror flips the clock horizontally, so mirrored positions pair up: 3:40 read backwards becomes 8:20. A quick check: mirror 12:00 reads 12:00 itself.
lessonContent:
Mirror reflections pair positions across the vertical axis.
Each apparent time has a fixed mirror partner summing around the dial.
Anchors like twelve o'clock — which reflects to itself — validate the method.
Symmetry turns guessing into mapping.

title: Four Months
question: Besides the ones with 31 days and short February, how many months have exactly 30 days?
correctExplanation: Right. April, June, September, and November each carry thirty days — four months of the year.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. The year partitions into seven thirty-one-day months, four thirty-day months, and February. Remembering the four — the ninth, fourth, sixth, and eleventh — completes the count.
lessonContent:
The calendar year partitions cleanly into three month lengths.
Mnemonics encode structure — knuckles for long months work.
Exhaustive listing prevents counting errors.
Calendar facts reward exact knowledge over impressions.

title: Sixty Days On
question: In a non-leap year, what date comes exactly 60 days after January 1?
correctExplanation: Exactly. January contributes thirty remaining days, February contributes twenty-eight, leaving two days into March.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is March 2. Sixty days after the first of January burns through the rest of January and all of February, landing on the second of March. Off-by-one errors come from counting January first as day zero or one — be consistent.
lessonContent:
Multi-month date arithmetic walks month by month with remainders.
January first is day one, not day zero — the classic slip.
Convert excess days into the next month's calendar positions.
Non-leap February keeps the arithmetic honest here.

title: Past Noon Overlap
question: After noon, when do the hour and minute hands of a clock next overlap? Give your answer to the nearest minute.
correctExplanation: Right. The minute hand needs slightly over sixty-five minutes to catch the hour hand after twelve sharp — about 1:05 and 27 seconds.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: about 1:05. The minute hand must lap a moving target, so the catch happens past one o'clock, not at one sharp. Exact pursuit gives 1:05:27 — the overlap drifts later each hour.
lessonContent:
Catch-up times drift later as the target hand moves.
Twelve equal catch-ups spread across twelve hours means each takes about sixty-five and a half minutes.
Pursuit problems always involve relative speed.
Estimates to the nearest minute suffice for hand puzzles.

title: The Gaining Clock
question: A clock gains three minutes every hour and was set correctly at midnight. What does it display when the true time is 6:00 PM?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Eighteen hours of gaining at three minutes per hour adds fifty-four minutes to the true six o'clock.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6:54 PM. Multiply the gain per hour by the elapsed hours: three times eighteen equals fifty-four. Fast clocks run ahead, so the display sits past the true time.
lessonContent:
Gaining clocks accumulate error in the forward direction.
Total error equals rate of gain times elapsed hours.
Convert the true time into hours from the last setting.
Add the error for gainers, subtract for losers.

title: Hidden in Words
question: What appears twice in every week, once in every year, but never in a single day?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Weeks carry two of them, years one, and days none — the answer hides in the spelling, not the calendar.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the letter E. Week contains two, year contains one, and day contains none. Letter-hiding puzzles redirect attention from meaning to spelling.
lessonContent:
Letter puzzles redirect attention from meaning to spelling.
Scan the words themselves, not what they represent.
Counting letters in each candidate word verifies quickly.

title: The Evening Train
question: A train departs at 18:47 and arrives at 21:13 the same evening. How long is the journey?
correctExplanation: Right. From 18:47 to 21:47 would be three hours; arriving 34 minutes earlier trims it to 2:26.
incorrectExplanation: The duration is 2 hours 26 minutes. Subtract hour from hour and minute from minute, borrowing when needed: 13 from 47 borrows an hour, giving 1 hour 34 minutes plus the remaining 1 hour — 2:26 total. Timetable arithmetic is subtraction with borrows.
lessonContent:
Timetable subtraction borrows across the sixtieth, not the tenth.
Work minutes first, then borrow an hour when needed.
Anchor to round times to sanity-check the total.
Converting to minutes first removes all borrowing risk.

title: Fourteen Days
question: How many weekdays appear in any span of exactly fourteen consecutive days, regardless of the starting day?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Fourteen days is exactly two full weeks, and every full week contributes five weekdays.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Any fourteen consecutive days contain exactly two of each weekday — two Saturdays, two Sundays — leaving ten weekdays. Full-week spans erase all dependence on the start.
lessonContent:
Full-week spans are immune to starting-day effects.
Two weeks guarantee exactly two of every weekday.
Multiples of seven neutralize calendar chance.
Guarantee questions seek structure immune to arrangement.

title: The Minute Hand's Day
question: In one full day, how many complete rotations does the minute hand of a clock make?
correctExplanation: Right. One rotation per hour times twenty-four hours in a day.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 24. The minute hand circles once each hour, and a day holds twenty-four hours. The common trap confuses it with the hour hand, which manages only two turns in the same day.
lessonContent:
Clock-hand rotation counts scale with their periods.
The minute hand spins once hourly; the hour hand once every twelve hours.
Match each hand to its own cycle length.
Scaling a per-hour rate to a day is multiplication by twenty-four.

title: Unlucky Thirteenths
question: In a single calendar year, what is the maximum number of Friday-the-13ths that can occur?
correctExplanation: Exactly. In the tightest calendar arrangements, three separate months can begin on a Sunday, yielding three unlucky Fridays.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. A Friday the thirteenth requires the month to open on a Sunday. Depending on the year's layout, at least one and at most three months manage it. Calendar structure caps the coincidence.
lessonContent:
Thirteenth-day questions reduce to month-start weekdays.
Each pattern of year-start weekdays fixes the possible coincidences.
Extremes of calendar puzzles follow from structure, not luck.
At least one per year is a pleasing guarantee.

title: The Century Exception
question: The year 2000 was a leap year even though 1900 was not, despite both being divisible by four. What extra rule included 2000?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Century years must clear the extra bar of dividing evenly by 400 — which 2000 clears and 1900 fails.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: divisible by 400. The Gregorian system drops three leap days every four centuries to stay synced with the year's true length. Divisible-by-four alone is not enough at century boundaries.
lessonContent:
The Gregorian calendar trims three leap days every four centuries.
Century years need divisibility by 400 to count as leap years.
2000 qualified; 2100 will not.
Small corrections keep calendars honest over millennia.

title: After Noon
question: What time is it 150 minutes after noon?
correctExplanation: Exactly. One hundred fifty minutes is two and a half hours, and half past two follows noon by exactly that.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2:30 PM. Divide minutes by sixty to get hours and leftover minutes: one hundred fifty makes two hours with thirty remaining. Minute-to-hour conversion is division with a remainder.
lessonContent:
Minutes convert to hours by dividing by sixty.
The remainder is the minute component of the answer.
Two-and-a-half-hour blocks are common time arithmetic.
Anchor conversions to noon or midnight for clarity.

title: The Summer Pair
question: Which two consecutive months of the year both have 31 days?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The calendar's long-pair sits mid-year: the seventh and eighth months each carry thirty-one days.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is July and August. Every other thirty-one-day month stands next to a shorter neighbor. Roman emperors each claimed a full month — a quirk fossilized in the modern calendar.
lessonContent:
Calendar structure carries historical fingerprints.
Consecutive thirty-one-day months are unique to mid-year.
Fossilized political decisions still shape modern date math.
Spotting calendar anomalies builds structural memory.

title: After the Holidays
question: One year, Christmas Eve falls on a Tuesday. What day of the week is January 6 of the following year?
correctExplanation: Right. Christmas Eve, New Year's Eve, and the week's rhythm all land on Tuesdays; January 1 is Wednesday, and the sixth falls six days later — Monday.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is Monday. December 31 is also a Tuesday, making January 1 a Wednesday; count six days forward to land on Monday. Crossing the year boundary changes nothing about weekday arithmetic.
lessonContent:
Year boundaries never disturb weekday arithmetic.
December 24 and December 31 share a weekday.
Anchoring on the first of the new month simplifies counting.
Cross-year puzzles test confidence more than skill.

title: The Bell Total
question: A grandfather clock strikes once at one o'clock, twice at two, and so on up to twelve. How many strikes sound in a full twelve-hour cycle?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The sum of one through twelve is the classic triangular number: half of twelve times thirteen.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 78. Pairing the hours — one with twelve, two with eleven, and so on — gives six pairs of thirteen, totalling seventy-eight. Pairing turns tedious addition into multiplication.
lessonContent:
Summing runs of numbers rewards the pairing trick.
One-through-n sums are triangular numbers: n times n-plus-one over two.
Gauss's famous schoolboy shortcut still wins races.
Structure spotting replaces long addition.

title: Leap-Day Birthdays
question: Someone born on February 29 counts only true leap-day birthdays. By their 25th actual birthday, how many leap-day birthdays have they celebrated?
correctExplanation: Right. Leap days arrive at ages 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 — six celebrations before twenty-five.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Within twenty-five years sit six leap years — at ages four through twenty-four in steps of four. Dividing twenty-four by four gives the count directly.
lessonContent:
Leap-day patterns step in fours.
Counting occurrences in a span is division with an endpoint check.
Twenty-five years hold six multiples of four.
Inclusive-versus-exclusive endpoints decide the last step.

title: Mid-Year Count
question: How many days pass from June 1 to July 1, inclusive of the start and exclusive of the end?
correctExplanation: Exactly. June carries thirty days, so the walk from its first day to the next month's first day covers exactly thirty.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 30. The count spans all of June, which holds thirty days. Stating endpoint conventions — included start, excluded end — prevents the classic off-by-one wobble.
lessonContent:
Date-difference puzzles hinge on endpoint conventions.
Stating inclusive or exclusive bounds prevents off-by-one errors.
Whole-month spans equal that month's length directly.

title: The Backward Clock
question: A clock runs backward at normal speed, starting correctly at noon. How often does its display show the correct time?
correctExplanation: Right. Running the wrong way, its error accumulates at double rate, and the display matches truth whenever the error wraps a full cycle — every 360 minutes.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: every six hours. The backward display errs two minutes per minute, and coincidence requires an accumulated offset of a full half-day. That threshold arrives every 360 minutes, giving four correct shows daily: noon, six, midnight, and six again.
lessonContent:
Backward-running clocks err at double rate.
Correct displays occur when accumulated error wraps a full cycle.
Wrapping arithmetic makes coincidence periodic.
Twelve-hour dials forgive offsets of exactly half a day.
